title: We Keep Trying to Save Instructional Time. We’re Accidentally Gutting It Instead.
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Stinehart argues that schools measure scheduled instructional minutes while ignoring instructional yield, the minutes in which children are actually engaged. Using the image of a 75-minute math block that takes 10 to 20 minutes to settle, and the line that nobody gets saved after noon, he claims the clock proves only that teaching was scheduled, not that learning occurred. He cites off-task and recess research, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, to argue that a short child-led play reset may recover more attention than it costs. He reframes classroom management as whack-a-mole against biological needs for movement, talk and autonomy, and borrows Gorski's structural lens: when many children struggle at the same point daily, the schedule belongs in the investigation. His practical step is modest: protect one reasonable play reset, count redirections, measure time-to-task, and compare what the schedule surrendered with what students gained. The bucket call is Practice & Culture because the piece is about behavior, routines and school-schedule culture rather than pedagogy.
points: Scheduled time is not engaged time: yield equals scheduled minutes minus lost minutes, and schools track only the first number.
Repeated redirections at the same point every day are data about the schedule design, not evidence of defective children.
Child-led play bundles movement, choice, social connection and freedom in one short break, unlike adult-led brain breaks.
The author's illustrative arithmetic suggests a ten-minute reset in a ninety-minute block could yield more real learning than the unbroken block.
The recommended first move is a small audit, not a new mandated program: protect one reset, count redirections, measure time-to-task.
quotes: It took me years in the classroom to realize something embarrassingly obvious: we may be saving instructional time on the schedule and then spending that same time buying children’s attention back one frustrated redirection at a time.
The clock can prove that instruction was scheduled. The clock cannot tell us how much learning actually occurred.
Scheduled minutes − lost minutes = instructional yield. Schools closely monitor the first number. We almost always ignore the subtraction.

When one child struggles unexpectedly, the child’s individual needs deserve attention. When large numbers of children struggle predictably at the same point every day, the schedule belongs in the investigation.
Same people. Different design. Different outcome. School schedules are designs too.
A school schedule is a policy document disguised as a grid. It determines when children may move, speak, interact, choose, create, recover, and use their bodies.
A ten-minute child-led play break looks like ten minutes taken away from teaching. Sometimes it may be the 10-minute break that gives the rest of the hour back.
